user_input: What's the difference between IsAuthenticated and AllowAny?

user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }

user_input: My API is getting hammered. I want to cap how many requests anonymous vs logged-in users can make per day. What's the mechanism and where do the numbers go?
reference: Enable AnonRateThrottle and UserRateThrottle as throttle classes and put the actual limits (like '100/day' and '1000/day') under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES.
reference_contexts: The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES settings.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle' , 'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle' ], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES' : { 'anon' : '100/day' , 'user' : '1000/day' } } The rates used in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.

user_input: Scrapers hit us in short violent bursts; our real users trickle requests out over the whole day. If I set the ceiling low enough to stop a burst I punish the real users, and if I set it high enough for the real users the bursts sail through. Can I enforce both shapes at once?
reference: Yes — stack two throttles instead of picking one number. Subclass UserRateThrottle twice and give each subclass its own unique `scope`, e.g. a `burst` class and a `sustained` class, then list both in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and define a rate for each scope under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES (something like '60/min' and '1000/day'). Multiple UserRateThrottles can be in force at the same time, and every request is checked against all of them, so a client has to stay under the short window and the long one simultaneously.
reference_contexts: An API may have multiple UserRateThrottles in place at the same time. To do so, override UserRateThrottle and set a unique "scope" for each class.
class BurstRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle): scope = 'burst' class SustainedRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle): scope = 'sustained'

user_input: When the payment provider we call during checkout is slow or down, our endpoint currently returns a wall of HTML with a stack trace in it. I want it to answer with a clean, machine-readable 'try again shortly' that our clients can branch on, and I want to define that once rather than writing the same try/except into every view that touches the provider.
reference: Define your own exception type and raise it; the framework turns it into the response. Subclass APIException — the base class for exceptions raised inside an APIView or @api_view — and set `.status_code`, `.default_detail` and `.default_code` on the class, e.g. a ServiceUnavailable with status_code = 503 and a default_detail of 'Service temporarily unavailable, try again later.'. Then any view that raises it produces that response, handled centrally instead of per view, and the body comes back in the standard error shape with a `detail` key rather than as a Django HTML error page. Note the boundary: this handling only applies to responses generated by *raised* exceptions — a Response object you return directly from a view, such as an explicit HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST, never passes through it.
reference_contexts: The base class for all exceptions raised inside an APIView class or @api_view.
To provide a custom exception, subclass APIException and set the .status_code, .default_detail, and .default_code attributes on the class.
Subclasses of APIException raised inside REST framework.

Note that the exception handler will only be called for responses generated by raised exceptions. It will not be used for any responses returned directly by the view, such as the HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST responses that are returned by the generic views when serializer validation fails.

user_input: Our mobile client only ever renders two columns from this endpoint but the payload carries about thirty, and on a slow connection that's the difference between a snappy list and a spinner. The web client needs the full object from the same endpoint. I'd rather not stand up a parallel serializer and a parallel URL just to serve a narrower version of the same record.
reference: You don't need a second serializer class — the field set is mutable at runtime. Once a serializer is initialized its fields are available as the `.fields` attribute, an ordinary dictionary you can read and modify, which lets you change what gets rendered (and the arguments on individual fields) per instance rather than at declaration time. The documented pattern is a DynamicFieldsModelSerializer: accept an extra `fields` keyword in __init__, pop it before calling super(), and then drop everything not requested from self.fields. Your view decides what to pass — typically driven by a query parameter — so UserSerializer(user) returns the full record and UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email')) returns the narrow one from the same class and the same URL. If you'd rather not hand-roll it, drf-dynamic-fields provides a mixin that limits fields from a URL parameter, and drf-flex-fields additionally handles expanding primitive fields into nested ones.
reference_contexts: Once a serializer has been initialized, the dictionary of fields that are set on the serializer may be accessed using the .fields attribute. Accessing and modifying this attribute allows you to dynamically modify the serializer.
Modifying the fields argument directly allows you to do interesting things such as changing the arguments on serializer fields at runtime, rather than at the point of declaring the serializer.

class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer): """ A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that controls which fields should be displayed. """ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None) # Instantiate the superclass normally super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
print(UserSerializer(user)) {'id': 2, 'username': 'jonwatts', 'email': 'jon@example.com'} print(UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email'))) {'id': 2, 'email': 'jon@example.com'}
The drf-dynamic-fields package provides a mixin to dynamically limit the fields per serializer to a subset specified by an URL parameter.

Renders data into HTML for the Browsable API: This renderer will determine which other renderer would have been given highest priority, and use that to display an API style response within the HTML page.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.renderers.JSONRenderer' , 'rest_framework.renderers.BrowsableAPIRenderer' , ] } You can also set the renderers used for an individual view, or viewset, using the APIView class-based views.

REST framework uses a simple style of content negotiation to determine which media type should be returned to a client, based on the available renderers, the priorities of each of those renderers, and the client's Accept: header.

Also note that although this class provides the complete set of create/list/retrieve/update/destroy actions by default, you can restrict the available operations by using the standard permission classes.

html_cutoff - If set this will be the maximum number of choices that will be displayed by a HTML select drop down. Set to None to disable any limiting. Defaults to 1000.

user_input: Our front-end is deployed on a completely different domain from the API. The browser fires off an OPTIONS request and then refuses to send the real one, and none of this ever reaches our view code — no log line, nothing. What's the supported way to let this through?
reference: That's a cross-origin problem, not an authentication one: the browser is refusing to hand the response to a client on another domain unless the server returns headers permitting it. DRF's recommendation is to add those headers in middleware rather than in your views, so CORS is supported transparently across the whole API without changing view behaviour. The docs point at Adam Johnson's `django-cors-headers` package, which is known to work correctly with REST framework.
reference_contexts: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a mechanism for allowing clients to interact with APIs that are hosted on a different domain. CORS works by requiring the server to include a specific set of headers that allow a browser to determine if and when cross-domain requests should be allowed.

The best way to deal with CORS in REST framework is to add the required response headers in middleware. This ensures that CORS is supported transparently, without having to change any behavior in your views.
Adam Johnson maintains the django-cors-headers package, which is known to work correctly with REST framework APIs.

user_input: I want some endpoints to render as real HTML pages using my own templates. What renderer supports that and what does the view return?

reference_contexts: The TemplateHTMLRenderer class expects the response to contain a dictionary of context data, and renders an HTML page based on a template that must be specified either in the view or on the response.
Additionally, serializers can be used as HTML forms and rendered in templates.
REST framework is suitable for returning both API style responses, and regular HTML pages.
Renders data to HTML, using Django's standard template rendering.

user_input: I want to combine two permission rules — e.g. authenticated OR a read-only request — without writing a whole new class. Is there a concise way?
reference: Yes: permission classes inheriting from BasePermission compose with Python's bitwise operators, so IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly works using &, | and ~.
reference_contexts: Provided they inherit from rest_framework.permissions.BasePermission , permissions can be composed using standard Python bitwise operators.

method in SAFE_METHODS class ExampleView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly ] def get ( self , request , format = None ): content = { 'status' : 'request was permitted' } return Response ( content ) Note Composition of permissions supports the & (and), | (or) and ~ (not) operators, and also allows the use of brackets ( ) to group expressions.
Operators follow the same precedence and associativity rules as standard logical operators ( ~ highest, then & , then | ).

user_input: We already run an OAuth 2.0 provider for our mobile apps, and I'd rather not stand up a second, parallel credential system inside the API just so the framework has something it recognises. Is there a supported way to have it accept the credentials we're already issuing?

reference: Two knobs, and the URL one is itself two values. The router picks up methods decorated with @action and generates routes for them, with `detail=True` or `detail=False` deciding whether the pattern carries a pk. By default the URL pattern comes from the method name and the URL *name* is the viewset's basename joined to the hyphenated method name — and `url_path` and `url_name` change those two independently. Changing only url_path leaves the reverse name as it was, so a serializer reversing the name you assumed gets NoReverseMatch; set both, or reverse the name that's actually registered. Permissions are separate: @action accepts `permission_classes`, e.g. @action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]). Two things stop those from firing. Object-level checks only run when the object is fetched through get_object(), so an action that queries the model directly never triggers them — call self.check_object_permissions() yourself if you do. And do not wire an @action method up with .as_view(): that bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings including permission_classes, which is the usual cause of a permission that appears to be attached but never runs.

By default, the URL pattern is based on the method name, and the URL name is the combination of the ViewSet.basename and the hyphenated method name. If you don't want to use the defaults for either of these values, you can instead provide the url_path and url_name arguments to the @action decorator.
